pedagogy.summary: Year 2 (age 6–7) money problems stay within a single unit (pence): totalling the cost of items, and — the demanding part — finding change and answering 'how much more do I need?'. The pedagogical key is that change is a DIFFERENCE, and young children find it far easier to reach a difference by COUNTING UP (the 'shopkeeper's method') with real coins than by counting back or by written take-away. Teaching should make change a practical, coin-in-hand act before it becomes an abstract subtraction.
bestPractices: Build change by counting UP from the price to the amount paid, using real or realistic coins so the coins themselves record each step (e.g. 35p → +5p = 40p → +10p = 50p; change 15p) — the DfE mental-calculation guidance calls this the shopkeeper's method and notes many children find counting up easier than counting back.
Model the same jumps on an empty number line so the change is seen as the TOTAL DISTANCE travelled (the sum of the jumps), not a point on the line.
Connect 'how much more do I need?' to the identical counting-up structure — it is the same gap read the other way — so children see missing-addend and change as one idea.
Keep amounts to manageable, 'friendly' values first (bridging one multiple of ten), then extend; use role-play shops so the procedure is rehearsed in a real context.
Press children to CHECK reasonableness — count the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid.
keyRepresentations: Real/realistic coins counted into the hand (coins as a record of the steps)
Empty number line showing change as jumps from price up to amount paid
Part–whole (bar) model: amount paid = cost + change
commonMisconceptions: 'More coins = more money' — thinks a fistful of small coins is worth more, so gives too many or judges having-enough by count not value.
Adds the two numbers (price + amount paid) instead of finding the difference, because early teaching over-emphasises 'take away' and difference is not recognised as subtraction.
Loses the running total or miscounts when bridging through a multiple of ten while counting up.
Counts single pennies one-by-one inaccurately instead of using coin values.

learn.summary: Year 2 (age 6–7) money problems stay within a single unit (pence): totalling the cost of items, and the more demanding work of finding change and answering 'how much more do I need?'. The core idea is that change is a DIFFERENCE, most easily reached by COUNTING UP from the price to the amount paid (the 'shopkeeper's method') with real coins, rather than by counting back or written take-away. Change should be a practical, coin-in-hand act before it becomes an abstract subtraction.

activities.title: Give change at a role-play market stall (count up with coins)
feedback: When your counting-on reaches the amount paid, confirm success: 'You've counted on to 50p — the 15p of change you built (10p + 5p), added to the 35p price, rebuilds the amount paid.' (Note the change coins total 15p; it is the running total counted on from the price that reaches 50p.)
If one coin too many goes in, show the running total overshooting the amount paid (past 50p) and invite the child to remove a coin and recount up.
If the running total is still short, point to the remaining gap: 'Counting on from 35p you've reached 40p — how much more to reach 50p?'

Optional live supports that make the mechanism visible: a running-total bar that starts at the price (35p) and rises with each coin to the amount paid (50p), and an empty number line on which each jump (+5, +10) draws itself from 35 up to 50.
activities.rationale: Counting up from the smaller to the larger value ('shopkeeper's method') is an easier route to a difference for many young children than counting back, and coins give a concrete record of each step. Physically building the change makes 'change as difference' felt before it is written.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should solve simple problems in a practical context involving addition and subtraction of money of the same unit, including giving change.

Change/difference is best found by counting UP from the smaller to the larger number ('shopkeeper's method'); many children find it easier to subtract by counting up than counting back, and coins provide a record of how the change was given (worked example: 27p, change from 50p = 3p + 20p = 23p).
learnerActions: Set up a shop: a toy priced 35p, a 50p coin to pay with, and a pot of mixed coins.
Count UP aloud from the price to the amount paid, placing a coin into a change tray at each step: '35… (put in a 5p) 40… (put in a 10p) 50'.
State the change as the coins you built: 'The change is 15p — a 10p and a 5p.'
Check by counting the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid (35p + 15p = 50p).
Repeat with other friendly prices (e.g. 45p paid with 50p gives 5p), then extend to the source worked example 27p paid with 50p, counting 27→30→50 to give 3p + 20p = 23p.
activities.intendedInsight: Change is the DISTANCE travelled from the price up to the amount paid — it is the total of the jumps you make when counting up (here 5p + 10p = 15p), not a take-away you have to work out on paper. The coins themselves record how the change was reached.

activities.title: 'How much more do I need?' — the same gap read the other way
feedback: Confirm when the count-up reaches the price exactly: '15 up to 20 is one jump of 5p — you need 5p more.'
If the child adds 15 + 20, re-anchor: 'You already have 15p; count on from there up to 20p to see what's missing.'
activities.rationale: Presenting change and missing-addend through the identical counting-up structure helps children treat the two situations as one move rather than as unrelated, and supports recognising difference (not only 'take away') as subtraction.
sourceClaims: Change/difference is best found by counting UP from the smaller to the larger number ('shopkeeper's method'); many children find it easier to subtract by counting up than counting back, and coins provide a record of how the change was given (worked example: 27p, change from 50p = 3p + 20p = 23p).
learnerActions: Set a toy priced 20p and give the child 15p.
Ask: 'How much MORE do you need to buy this?'
Count UP from what you have to the price: '15… (add a 5p) 20' and name the shortfall as 5p.
Line this up against a change task: notice that finding the shortfall and finding change are the same counting-up move, just started from a different amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding change and finding 'how much more I need' (missing addend) are one idea: closing the gap by counting up between two amounts.

activities.title: Value, not number of coins
feedback: When the child checks totals: 'A fistful of pennies can be worth less than one coin — it's the value that counts, not the number.'
Praise finding several coin combinations that make the same value.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses the common 'more coins = more money' misconception by making children compare totals by value and build equal values from different combinations.
sourceClaims: A common money misconception to address explicitly is 'if I have the most coins I will always have the most money'; children may confuse one pence and one pound, and value should not be judged by coin count or size.
learnerActions: Lay the child's handful of small coins beside a single 10p and 5p.
Count the total VALUE of each set and compare, e.g. show that ten 1p coins are worth less than one 20p.
Make the SAME value (e.g. 15p) with different coin combinations (10p + 5p; 5p + 5p + 5p; 10p + 2p + 2p + 1p).
activities.intendedInsight: Money is judged by total value, not by how many coins there are; many small coins can be worth less than one larger coin.

activities.title: Short written check on change and coin combinations
feedback: Mark correct amounts and valid combinations; for a wrong amount, send the child back to count up from the price with coins.
Note: a right answer here does not show the counting-up method — observe the hands-on building to assess the process.
activities.rationale: A brief recognition/short-answer check can confirm the answer, but it does not elicit the counting-up construction that is the heart of the objective, so it supplements rather than replaces hands-on work.
learnerActions: Given a price and an amount paid, state the change and the coins that make it.
Pick, from a set of options, coins that make a given change, and set a value (e.g. with a slider) to match the change for a given purchase.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick check confirms whether the child can land the correct change amount and a valid coin combination.

constraints: Keep amounts to friendly values that bridge a single multiple of ten first (e.g. 35p→50p), then extend once secure.
A tap-to-reveal picture of coins can serve as a reference to coin values; it does not let the child carry out or get feedback on the counting-up procedure, so it is a scaffold, not the main activity.
Recognition/short-answer checks assess the answer, not the method; they do not elicit the independent counting-up construction that is the objective.
Running-total bars (anchored at the price), number-line jumps, and a change tray are optional supports to make the gap visible — offer them to illustrate the mechanism, not as mandatory steps.

Keep the value of the change coins distinct from the running total: the change coins total the difference (e.g. 15p), while the running total counted on from the price reaches the amount paid (e.g. 50p).
Always have the child check reasonableness by counting the change back onto the price to rebuild the amount paid.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: change 15p = 10p + 5p and 35p + 15p = 50p; worked example 27p→50p = 3p + 20p = 23p; 45p→50p = 5p; missing-addend 15p→20p = 5p; ten 1p = 10p < one 20p; 15p = 10p+5p = 5p+5p+5p = 10p+2p+2p+1p. All consistent.
The 27p→50p worked example crosses more than one ten boundary, so it is presented as an extension of the friendly single-ten cases rather than as itself a single-ten bridge.

Value/running-total distinction maintained in the first activity: change coins total 15p, whereas the running total counted on from the 35p price reaches 50p; no wording states the change coins 'add up to 50p'.

The source labelled a 3D shop rendering as adding 'handling friction' and a role-play conversation as unsuited; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than restated as universal limits. A spoken shopkeeper exchange could in fact narrate the counting-up steps.

One cited source (NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives / Subtraction as difference') is marked verified:false in the row; the principle it supports (difference under-recognised because 'take away' is over-emphasised) is retained only as rationale framing, not cited as established evidence.

The original 'adds price + amount paid (35 + 50)' and 'counts single pennies inaccurately' misconceptions are addressed indirectly rather than as standalone correctives; a future revision could add an explicit change-activity prompt contrasting adding with finding the gap.

probeDeeper: 'Show me how you know that's the right change — can you count it back onto the 35p to make 50p again?'
'You gave me these coins; is there a way to make the same change with fewer coins?'
'What if the toy cost 32p instead of 35p — would the change be more or less? Why?'
'How is finding my change like working out how much MORE you need to buy the 20p toy?'
assess.correctAnswer: For change: counts up from 35p (e.g. +5p to 40p, +10p to 50p) and hands back 15p in coins, or otherwise establishes the 15p gap and gives it by value. For the second: identifies the 5p shortfall by counting on from 15p to 20p. In both, the coins/steps show a DIFFERENCE being built, and the child can check by rebuilding the paid amount.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'More coins means more money' — hands back a fistful of small coins and treats having given MANY coins as having given enough, judging by count not value ('I gave you loads, so that's enough').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to value: line up the child's handful against a single 10p+5p and count both totals; show that ten 1p is worth less than one 20p. Rehearse making the SAME value with different coin combinations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives too many low-value coins for the change, or is satisfied by the NUMBER of coins rather than checking their total value against the 15p gap.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two numbers instead of finding the difference — computes 35 + 50 = 85 (or grabs 85p) because 'take away' is the only subtraction they recognise and change isn't seen as subtraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act it out as a shopkeeper: physically count coins UP from 35p into the customer's hand to 50p, and name the total handed over as the change. Contrast 'the shop keeps 35p, you get the rest' with adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Combines the price and the amount paid; hands over far too much, or writes 35+50.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counting up but losing the running total when bridging a ten — reaches 40p, then miscounts the second jump (e.g. calls the change 10p or 25p).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: record each jump on an empty number line so the two jumps (+5, +10) are visible and can be added deliberately; keep amounts bridging a single ten until secure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts a correct counting-on path but the total of the jumps is wrong at the multiple-of-ten boundary.

responseLevels.gap: Grabs coins without matching value, adds the two amounts, or cannot establish the change; judges 'enough' by number of coins.
responseLevels.full: Reliably builds change by counting up from price to paid amount, solves the missing-addend 'how much more' by the same move, checks by rebuilding the paid amount, and transfers to a new price.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the change for the friendly case by counting up, but loses the total when bridging a ten, or can do the change but not the equivalent 'how much more do I need?', treating them as unrelated.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a toy labelled 35p and give the child a single 50p coin and a pot of mixed coins. Say: 'Buy the toy and give me the right change — use the coins to show me how you work it out.' Then set a second toy at 20p and say: 'You have 15p. How much more do you need to buy this one?' Watch HOW they work, not just the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands change as a difference counts UP from price to paid amount and the coins record the gap; a child who does not either adds 35+50, grabs a random fistful of coins judging 'enough' by how many, or counts back and loses the total. Correct reasoning yields 15p by a visible counting-on path; the wrong ideas each yield a different, diagnosable move.
